newsitem.title: CHINA: Old HK Bank building in Shanghai gets facelift.
newsitem.headline: Old HK Bank building in Shanghai gets facelift.

text.p: The most magnificent building of old Shanghai -- the former Hongkong & Shanghai Bank building on the waterfront Bund -- has been given a facelift to celebrate the return of Hong Kong to Chinese control, and to ready it for its new role as a Chinese bank.
British architects Donald Insall and Associates have been retained to renovate the entire structure, opened in 1925, which was leased last year by Shanghai's state-owned Pudong Development Bank.
"The aim is to complete the task and have part of the building open again as a bank later this year," said Anthony Close-Smith, the architect in charge of restoration work on the project.
"It's the most challenging assignment of my life due to the tight time schedules," he added.
Most of the building's facade was cleaned with special chemicals over a period of just 21 days in order to be ready for the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight last Monday.
"More than 100 workers were involved at any one time. It is probably the fastest conservation clean of a building of this size ever," Close-Smith said.

The architect, who is also responsible for the reconstruction of much of the British Royal Family's Windsor Castle, badly damaged in a fire in 1992, described the old Hongkong bank as a "sleeping beauty".
"It's had a very interesting history with many different owners which it has accommodated surprisingly well," he said. "It was very well built in the first place."
The bank was opened with much pomp and ceremony in 1923, the most potent symbol of the British Empire's financial might in the Far East.

The Japanese occupied it briefly in the early 1940s, and in the early 1950s, it became the Communist Party headquarters for Shanghai, a role it maintained until city officials moved to a new building in 1994.

The city government tried to get the Hongkong Bank to take back the building, but they failed to agree on a price, and no other foreign banks showed interest. It remained empty until the Pudong Bank agreed to lease it late last year.
"What is unique about this building is that so many others of its ilk, for instance in Hong Kong, have been demolished," said Close-Smith. "It's dusty, but many of the original features remain."
The lions which once flanked the bank's entrance are now in the city's historical museum, and it is not known if they will resume their original positions on the Bund as part of the renovation work.

The main banking hall, with its magnificent marble pillars and curved glass roof, is still much as it was, although the banking counters have been removed. The murals which adorned the main domed entrance hall have been plastered over.
